static_traits.name: Li Yuanhang
static_traits.family_status: Has a daughter who recently graduated from university (about 6 months ago)
static_traits.social_status: Has a few friends to talk to, but has not yet shared her sense of inadequacy and self-criticism with them
static_traits.medical_history: Without significant physical illness; without prior psychotherapy or counseling history; such problems have not yet occurred before
static_traits.language_features: Clear expression, fairly good logic, negative tone with self-reproach; highly focused on mileage data when running, prone to comparison and negating positive evidence; skeptical attitude toward change but reasonably cooperative

basic_info.main_problem: Persistently feeling 'poor physical fitness''not good enough' because she can only run two miles a day, despite having completed three triathlons; this produces strong self-criticism and dissatisfaction, affecting overall well-being and enjoyment of the activity.
basic_info.core_demands: Realizes that self-critical thinking is affecting overall well-being and enjoyment of activities, so hopes to explore and challenge these thoughts through counseling.
growth_experiences: About 6 months ago, after her daughter graduated from university and left home, entering the empty-nest stage, the client began to feel greater loneliness and stress; since then running has changed from a previous 'release' to a source of 'failure', each run focusing on the distance she can cover and reinforcing self-criticism, with an overall decline in sense of well-being.

Had participated in three triathlons, with a certain athletic foundation and endurance experience; but in comparison with other runners/participants, gradually formed stricter self-judgment standards, ignoring past achievements and efforts, making 'mileage' the single indicator for measuring self-worth.

special_situations.event: When running daily, only focuses on the distance one can run (usually stops at two miles)
special_situations.conditional_assumptions: If I cannot run more than two miles, it means I am not up to standard, not good enough
special_situations.compensatory_strategies: Constantly setting higher exercise goals and trying to increase mileage, while seeking others' approval to prove herself
special_situations.automatic_thoughts: Only being able to run two miles is pathetic, I am really no good

special_situations.event: Compares his performance with triathletes or others in the running community
special_situations.conditional_assumptions: If I am not as good as others, it equals failure, meaning I am not good enough
special_situations.compensatory_strategies: Practices extra to catch up with others, avoids talking about their own grades in social settings, or seeks external praise to raise self-evaluation
special_situations.automatic_thoughts: Everyone is stronger than me, I am not as good as others

special_situations.event: After her daughter graduated from university and the home became empty-nest, feeling unbalanced about changes in her role and state
special_situations.conditional_assumptions: As an adult/father, I should always maintain high levels of self-discipline and fitness, otherwise it proves I am not competent
special_situations.compensatory_strategies: Treats running performance as the main source of self-worth, constraining oneself with high standards
special_situations.automatic_thoughts: Since my daughter graduated I have become no good, which shows I am not good enough

special_situations.conditional_assumptions: If I feel tired, it means I am in poor shape, unhealthy
special_situations.compensatory_strategies: Continuing to ruminate and blame oneself after running, treating fatigue as evidence of failure
special_situations.automatic_thoughts: I am tired = I am terrible

core_conflict.wish: Longs to be recognized and to have one's own worth and competence seen, maintaining a sense of control over life and body
core_conflict.fear: Fearing being compared as not as good as others, being denied and ignored, worrying about losing meaning and role belonging (declining self-worth after the empty nest)
defense_goal: Maintains a sense of control through harsh self-standards and self-criticism
Uses running results and mileage as the main indicators of self-worth
Avoids exposing vulnerability to friends to prevent judgment or loss of face

object_relations.self_representation: A not-good-enough failure, a person with poor fitness
object_relations.object_representation: Others (runners / participants) are superior evaluators and comparison targets

object_relations.self_representation: A lonely empty-nest father, struggling to maintain past roles and sense of worth
object_relations.object_representation: External and family roles hold the expectation that I 'should always stay excellent'

behavioral_response_patterns.trigger_condition: When the counselor proposes changing the evaluation method and designing behavioral experiments to challenge negative thinking
behavioral_response_patterns.interpretation: Believing these methods may be ineffective for her, worrying about proving herself 'not good enough' once again (anticipatory doubt about failure)
behavioral_response_patterns.response_instruction: Use a steady, empathic tone, acknowledging her concerns; use gentle inquiry and concretizing questions, inviting her to start with small steps, and emphasizing the controllability and reversibility of the experiment.

behavioral_response_patterns.trigger_condition: When the counselor invites her to examine evidence and consider measures beyond mileage (such as endurance, subjective feelings, recovery)
behavioral_response_patterns.interpretation: Tends to talk about problems only in terms of mileage and data, avoiding emotional-level experience and vulnerable feelings
behavioral_response_patterns.response_instruction: Gentle tone with an experiential focus, encouraging her to name present feelings; use concrete experiential questions (e.g. 'where in the body does fatigue feel strongest?'), gradually introducing emotional and bodily experience while affirming her logic.

manifestations: After her daughter's graduation, entering the empty-nest stage, feeling lonelier and more stressed
Running changes from a former release into evidence of self-failure
Running, once a source of meaning and joy, no longer satisfies, and is instead dominated by a sense of failure
Measuring self-worth by the single metric of mileage leads to impoverished experience

contact_model.definition: The individual has poor self-reflection with excessive self-restriction / reproach, and is overly cautious about contact, corresponding to 'autonomy'.
manifestations: Excessively harsh and cautious judgment of one's own performance
Takes mileage as the only standard; carefully audits self
Skeptical about change; worried about failing again

contact_model.definition: The individual takes external rules and expectations as her own standards or absolute truth without digesting them, corresponding to 'refusal'.
manifestations: Uses 'should' as the standard of judgment (such as 'this ought to be easy')
Internalizing high standards as self-demands without examining them

positive_force: Has completed three triathlons in the past, with training experience and an endurance foundation
Willing to try behavioral experiments and gradually adjust evaluation methods
Able to notice his pattern of over-focusing on mileage
Has some friends; potential social support resources exist
negative_force: Excessive self-criticism and frequent comparison with others
Relying on external recognition to confirm self-worth (seeking external validation)
Mental filtering and negating positive evidence
Emotional reasoning that treats fatigue as failure
Loneliness and stress brought by the empty nest, weakening the sense of self-meaning

target_behavior.behavior: Excessive focus on mileage when running and self-denial (self-criticism and dissatisfaction)
antecedent: Each time going out for a run
Seeing others run farther or faster
Not yet reaching self-set mileage standards (e.g. more than two miles)
target_behavior.core_reason: Loneliness and stress triggered by the empty-nest transition; comparison with others making self-worth dependent on external standards; cognitive distortions (mental filtering, negating the positive, personalization) reducing mileage to a single measure of success and failure
target_behavior.function: Maintaining a temporary sense of control and motivation through self-reproach and raising standards, and seeking external recognition to relieve the anxiety of 'I am not good enough'
target_behavior.consequence: Exercise enjoyment markedly declines, mood is impaired and dissatisfaction worsens, overall happiness lowered, daily exercise and sense of achievement affected
